ratings.why: A garbled body that crashes the process or returns 500 takes down every group's service and is a defect anyone would report.
Missing fields are the most common bad request, and a throw into a 500 or a dead process instead of a 400 is a plain defect.
Wrong-typed values should be refused rather than coerced or crash, but it is a smaller cost than missing-field handling since the 400 list already covers non-integer amounts.
A group created with an id containing '/' or similar that can never be addressed again is a real loss, though most clients use simple ids.
The request says whole cents, and a negative or fractional share silently moves debt the wrong way or breaks integer balances.
The request asks for two distinct names, so a careful builder dedupes or refuses duplicates and blanks, which change an equal split.
The request already says each member listed in shares owes that amount, so an omitted member owing nothing is the plain reading.
The customer was promised that data survives a restart and no expense is lost, so an acknowledged expense not yet on disk or a torn file loses data.
The first start on an empty machine has no file, and failing there breaks the service before it is ever used.
Silently replacing a corrupt file with an empty store would wipe data, so a careful builder refuses to start or says what was chosen.
The request defines DATA_FILE as the place the data lives, so behaviour when an operator omits it is a reasonable thing to leave unhandled.
The request says it listens on PORT, and handling missing or bad values is operator convenience rather than a requirement.
The request explicitly says concurrent requests must never lose an expense, and duplicate or skipped numbers make the ledger wrong.
In single-threaded Node with in-memory state a read naturally sees a consistent snapshot, so this needs no deliberate handling.
Two simultaneous creates of one id should give one 201 and one 409, which an async write path can get wrong.
Restarting the numbering would give two expenses the same number in one group, breaking the persistence promise.
Unknown paths and wrong methods should get a clean 404 or 405 rather than a hang or crash, though the exact status is a smaller matter.
JSON responses should carry application/json so clients parse them correctly, a small but real cost if wrong.
The request only specifies the 201 status for group creation, so the body or a Location header is a builder's choice.
The request specifies statuses only, so the shape of an error body is taste.
Which status wins is a choice, but a retry with a bad body must not replace the stored members, which a careful builder guards.
The request says every route under an unknown group answers 404, so checking the group first is the natural reading.
Ignoring extra fields is the default for a small JSON service, and applying shares on an equal split is an unlikely mistake.
Accepting a JSON body regardless of the Content-Type header is the ordinary choice, and the request does not ask for either.
A GET that changes stored debts would destroy the ledger on a poll, a plain defect anyone would report.
A file the server cannot read back to the same balances, settlements and next number breaks the persistence promise.
The next maintainer needs node --test to pass on a fresh checkout without a fixed port or a real data file.
Rolling back cleanly after a full disk or unwritable file is beyond what this small service request asks for.
Amounts beyond 9e15 cents are not realistic for shared expenses, so handling them is over-engineering.
A body size limit is hardening beyond the scope of this small service.
Whole-file rewrites that drop each other's changes would lose an expense or group, which the request explicitly forbids.
Names like constructor or __proto__ breaking balances is a real defect a careful builder avoids with a Map or null-prototype object, though such names are rare.
JSON.parse already turns 1.0 and 1e2 into integers, so this needs no deliberate handling.
With no id rules given in the request, a later id restriction cutting off stored groups is speculation.
A dropped connection mid-body should not crash the process or store a half-read expense, though Node's defaults mostly cover it.
The request names no Node version, and a dependency-free service on current Node is a reasonable default.
